extracted.intended_audience: academic researchers and authors (especially biomedical) deciding where to publish
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for authors on how to identify characteristics of predatory (fraudulent/deceptive) journals and steps/resources to verify journal credibility before submitting. Focus is on practical checks (website, emails, indexing, fees, editorial board) and tools to avoid scams.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims to be a peer reviewed open access publication but does not provide adequate peer review or the level of peer review promised
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal claims to be peer reviewed/open access but fails to provide robust or the promised level of peer review (some predatory journals repeatedly use a template as their peer review report).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for clear description of peer review process, sample review reports, reviewer identities (where appropriate), and independent evidence (e.g., articles showing rigorous review). Beware of templated review reports or claims without detail. Use resources (ThinkCheckSubmit, COPE) to verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Advertises a Journal Impact Factor or other citation metric on the website that is incorrect or cannot be verified
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal advertises JIF or other citation metrics that are false, misleading, or not verifiable via established sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify metrics through Journal Citation Reports, SCImago, or the indexing service claimed. Be skeptical of proprietary/unknown metrics or badges that lack provenance; cross-check with Web of Science/Clarivate or SCImago.

rubrics_metrics.name: May advertise an unrealistic timeline for publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal advertises unusually fast timelines for peer review and publication which may be unrealistic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare promised timelines to norms in your field; extremely fast guarantees can indicate lack of proper peer review. Combine this check with inspection of actual published article dates and review histories when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishes all articles for which authors pay an APC even if the article is low quality, unrelated to the topic of the journal, or nonsensical
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal appears to accept and publish any submission as long as the author pays the Article Processing Charge, regardless of quality or relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine recent issues/archives for off-topic content, low-quality or nonsensical articles. If many articles are irrelevant or poor quality, this suggests pay-to-publish practice rather than selective peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishes articles that have many grammar mistakes (little or no copyediting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Published articles contain numerous grammatical errors and show evidence of minimal or no copyediting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Browse the journal's published articles for consistent copyediting issues. Poor editorial standards across issues suggest predatory behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial board includes people who do not exist, do not have credentials relevant to the topic of the journal, have affiliations that cannot be verified, or are real people who are not aware that they are listed as members
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial board lists unverifiable or inappropriate members, fabricated names, incorrect credentials, or people listed without consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify editorial board members by checking their institutional webpages, publication records, and contacting them if necessary. Watch for generic names, lack of affiliations, or individuals unaware of their listing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mimics name or website of other well-known, legitimate journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal name, website design, or branding closely imitates established legitimate journals to confuse authors/readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare journal title and URL carefully to known journals; look for small differences, misspellings, or look-alike domains. Confirm publisher identity via established catalogs (NLM Catalog, DOAJ).

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggressively targets potential authors through emails
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal or publisher sends frequent, flattering, or mass solicitation emails encouraging submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate solicitation emails critically: mass mailings, generic salutations, or promises to publish anything are red flags. Track unsolicited invitations and compare to field norms; consult colleagues or librarian if unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: May state that offices are in one country but contact details are in another
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal lists inconsistent geographic/contact information (different office country vs contact details).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify physical address and phone numbers; check country codes and institutional affiliations. Inconsistencies may indicate fraudulent or opaque operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation emails contain grammatical errors of phishing scams
rubrics_metrics.description: Emails soliciting submissions contain obvious grammatical mistakes, awkward phrasing, or other signs typical of phishing/spam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat solicitation emails with poor language as suspicious. Cross-check sender domain, look for mismatches, and verify the journal via independent sources before responding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of transparency about acceptance process or APCs, so that authors do not know how much they will be charged until their article is accepted
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal does not clearly state acceptance criteria, peer review process, or Article Processing Charges; fees are revealed only after acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require clear APC and acceptance policy information before submission. Legitimate journals state fees up front and explain review/acceptance steps. Absence of transparency is a major red flag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requires authors sign away their copyright to the article at the time of submission, making it impossible for the author to submit the article to another publisher
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher demands transfer of copyright upon submission rather than after acceptance, restricting authors' rights prematurely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read submission and copyright terms carefully. Do not submit if the publisher demands copyright transfer at submission; legitimate publishers typically request copyright/license agreements after acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishes articles submitted before the authors have signed the publishing agreement, then refuses to take the article down if the author withdraws the submission
rubrics_metrics.description: Journal posts articles prior to finalized publishing agreements and may refuse to remove content if authors withdraw.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid publishers who publish before agreements are in place. Retain records and consult COPE guidance or institutional librarians if you encounter refusal to remove withdrawn work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removes articles or entire journals from the web without warning or informing authors
rubrics_metrics.description: Publisher may take down articles or journals unpredictably, sometimes removing authors' published work without notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check stability of journal archives and publisher reputation. Be wary if archives are incomplete, inconsistent, or disappear; such behavior risks loss of the scholarly record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine the journal's archives for off-topic, low-quality, or nonsensical articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Look through past issues/contents to judge the fit, quality, and topical focus of published articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If archives contain many irrelevant, incoherent, or poor-quality items, consider this a sign the journal accepts articles indiscriminately. Use this as practical evidence of editorial standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Are there spelling or grammatical mistakes or other questionable characteristics on their website or in the solicitation email?
rubrics_metrics.description: Check the journal website and solicitation correspondences for spelling, grammar, or other obvious quality issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poor website copy, broken links, inconsistent design, or obvious language errors suggest low professional standards and possible predatory intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the peer review process clearly stated on the website?
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the journal provides a clear description of its peer review processes and criteria.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legitimate journals describe review type (single/double/blind), expected timeline, reviewer selection, and editorial oversight. Lack of such information is suspicious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the website clearly state the publishing fees?
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the journal transparently lists Article Processing Charges and other fees publicly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparent fee schedules are standard for reputable OA journals. Hidden or vaguely described fees that are revealed only after acceptance are a warning sign.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the journal indexed in databases that you use, such as MEDLINE?
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify whether the journal is indexed in appropriate, reputable bibliographic databases for your field (e.g., MEDLINE for biomedical journals).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use NLM Catalog to check MEDLINE indexing; remember PubMed appearance does not equal MEDLINE indexing. Lack of indexing is not definitive but can be an indicator when combined with other red flags.

rubrics_metrics.name: Can you easily contact the publisher?
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the publisher provides reliable, verifiable contact information (email, phone, address).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test contact channels; verify phone country code and whether emails/time-stamps match claimed location. Difficult or inconsistent contact info is concerning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Are the time-stamps of incoming emails consistent with the working hours of the reported country of origin?
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether solicitation/communication timestamps align with the publisher's claimed country/time zone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inconsistencies between claimed location and actual email timestamps may indicate deceptive operations or misrepresented geography.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the phone number have the correct country code?
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify that listed phone numbers include appropriate country codes for the publisher's claimed location.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorrect or missing country codes are a simple factual check; mismatches can indicate false claims about office location.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the journal a member of COPE, OASPA, or listed in DOAJ?
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the journal/publisher is a member of recognized professional organizations (Committee on Publication Ethics, Open Access Scholarly Publishers Association) or listed in the Directory of Open Access Journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership or listing in COPE, OASPA, or DOAJ is supportive evidence of legitimacy but verify authenticity of the membership/listing. Use those organizations' own sites to confirm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicitation email characteristics: flattering language and promises to publish anything
rubrics_metrics.description: Solicitation emails that are overly flattering and promise to publish any submission may indicate predatory solicitation tactics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat such promises skeptically. Legitimate journals typically do not promise acceptance; consult colleagues or librarians when in doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vetted tools/resources and consult librarians to verify journal quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ checklists and databases (ThinkCheckSubmit, DOAJ, COPE, SCImago, NLM Catalog, Stop Predatory Journals, Cabells, Journal Citation Reports) and ask institutional or local librarians for assistance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ThinkCheckSubmit.org for step-by-step evaluation; check DOAJ for reputable OA journals; verify indexing via NLM Catalog/SCImago; use Cabells and JCR where available; be aware of limitations (e.g., anonymity or lack of transparency in some crowdsourced lists). When uncertain, ask a librarian for help.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of publishing in predatory journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing in predatory journals can lead to fake peer review undermining scientific discourse, reduced discoverability and citation, and risk of being scammed or losing control of your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider these negative outcomes when evaluating a journal—loss of credibility, inability of peers to find/use your work, removal of articles, or inability to submit elsewhere. Use this as motivation to perform the checks above before submission.
